question: Two wires A and B are made of same material and have the same length but different cross-sectional areas. If the resistance of wire A is 9 times the resistance of wire B, the ratio of the radius of wire A to that of wire B is:
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 ∶ 3**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **1 ∶ 3** is the ratio of the radius of wire A to that of wire B.
 
• Since the wires A and B are made of the same material and have the same length, their resistances depend solely on their cross-sectional areas.
 
• The resistance R of a wire is given by the formula R = \frac{\rho L}{A} , where \rho is the resistivity, L is the length, and A is the cross-sectional area.
 
• If the resistance of wire A is 9 times the resistance of wire B, then R_A = 9R_B .
 
• Given R \propto \frac{1}{A} , we have \frac{A_B}{A_A} = 9 , meaning the cross-sectional area of wire B is 9 times that of wire A.
 
• Since the cross-sectional area A of a wire is proportional to the square of its radius r (i.e., A \propto r² ), we have \frac{r_B²}{r_A²} = 9 .
 
• Taking the square root of both sides, \frac{r_B}{r_A} = 3 , hence the ratio \frac{r_A}{r_B} = \frac{1}{3} .
 
• Therefore, the ratio of the radius of wire A to that of wire B is **1 ∶ 3**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **resistance of a wire is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area**.
 
• For wires of the same material and length, a wire with a larger cross-sectional area will have a lower resistance.
 
• The concept of resistance and its dependence on **material, length, and cross-sectional area **is fundamental in understanding electrical circuits and materials science.
